newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks to fall, opportunity to buy-Paribas.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks to fall, opportunity to buy-Paribas.

text.p: Indian stock markets are seen falling further in the next few months, offering a buying opportunity, Paribas Capital Markets said on Friday.
"It could go down further in the next couple of months on earnings disappointments, more depressing economic statistics, and more negative political headlines," it said in a report.
"We think the (Bombay Stock Exchange) sensex could go below the 3,000 mark quite easily," Paribas analyst Rupa Bose said.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-share index plunged 98.41 points on October 7 to 3,002.86 but has since revived, closing at 3,126.34 on Thursday.

Nevertheless, the Indian market is trading at quite a low P/E (Price/Earning ratio) relative to other Asian markets and other emerging markets, while consensus forecast growth rates are higher, the report said.
"Even adjusting for possible over-optimism among analysts, we think the expected growth will be at least in line with other Asian countries," it said.
"The period of low price may present a buying opportunity -- between six to 12 months from now, the market could rise quite sharply, perhaps crossing the 3,800 level," it said.
Bose said her optimism was based on the following:
+ Assuming the government uses the busy season credit policy to ease money supply, liquidity could start to feed into the system in about three to six months.
+ Many companies will find the second half of 1996/97 (April-March) better than the first half. While liquidity is far from easy, it is not as tight as it was a year ago.
+ Investors would have already factored in the impact of the minimum tax imposed in the July budget. In any case, within six months, investors will focus on 1997/98.
+ Political uncertainty will not necessarily block a market rise. If sentiment is positive, investors may well consider that the political downside is limited.
"Any political party will recognise the economic imperatives of the situation, and none wish to roll back liberalisation," the report said.
